where: Section 1, explanation after the p = N_V exp[−(E_F − E_V)/k_BT] formula
problem: The direction is stated backwards. The text says 'the further E_F is below the valence states, the fewer empty states there are'. In fact, pushing E_F further below E_V makes the exponent −(E_F − E_V)/k_BT large and positive, so p grows: more empty states. A student will take away the opposite trend from the one the formula gives.
fix: The exponent is negative because a hole is an empty state: the further E_F lies above the valence band edge, the smaller the hole concentration; pushing E_F down towards and below E_V gives more empty states and more holes.

problem: 'At low temperature n → N_D' contradicts the freeze-out bullet just above it, which says n falls as T falls because donors stay unionised. The formula assumes full ionisation (N_D⁺ = N_D), so it cannot describe freeze-out at all; it tends to N_D whenever n_i << N_D (which includes room temperature), and to n_i whenever n_i >> N_D. As written the two statements cannot both be true.
fix: This solution assumes full ionisation. When n_i << N_D (the extrinsic range) n → N_D; when n_i >> N_D (the intrinsic range) n → n_i. Below the freeze-out temperature the donors are not fully ionised and this formula no longer applies.

where: Section 1, symbols listed under n = N_C exp[−(E_C − E_F)/k_BT]
problem: The energies are given in eV but k_B is given as 1.381×10⁻²³ J/K, so the formula as printed mixes units. Only the later remark that k_BT = 0.0259 eV at 300 K saves it.
fix: State k_B = 8.617×10⁻⁵ eV/K (equivalently 1.381×10⁻²³ J/K) so that k_BT comes out in eV when the energies are in eV, and note that at 300 K k_BT = 0.0259 eV.

where: Section 3, line under the exact-solution formula
problem: The line begins 'where:' but no symbol is being defined; it is a comment on the formula. The 'where:' convention is used everywhere else for symbol meanings, so this reads as a slip.
fix: Drop 'where:' and write the comment as a plain sentence: 'This is the exact solution of n = N_D + n_i²/n, with p = n_i²/n to follow.'

problem: 'below the conduction band edge by a few k_BT' understates the size: at N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ the gap is about 0.21 eV, roughly 8k_BT. The phrase can mislead a student into thinking the Fermi level is always a tiny fraction of an eV from the band.
fix: Say the Fermi level sits below the conduction band edge by k_BT ln(N_C/N_D), typically a few tenths of an eV in silicon (about 0.2 eV at N_D = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³), i.e. several k_BT.
